prompt: What does an API key tell the server?
hint: Who else might hold the same string?

choices.text: Which person is making the request
choices.why: Everyone who holds the string looks the same to the server; a key cannot tell people apart.

choices.text: Which program is calling
choices.why: Right. Any person or script holding it is the same caller.

choices.text: How long the caller may keep using the API
choices.why: A key has no expiry of its own; that is what a token adds.

choices.text: Which orders the caller placed
choices.why: boxoffice's key opens a sales report and knows nothing of orders.

prompt: The sales report, asked with no key, answered 401 with a problem body. Why does the lesson still call it a defect?
hint: Compare its headers with the orders' 401.

choices.text: A missing key should be 400, since the request is incomplete
choices.why: Missing credentials are exactly what 401 is for.

choices.text: It should be 403, because the caller is not staff
choices.why: 403 is for a caller the server knows; with no key, it knows nobody.

choices.text: It leaves out the www-authenticate header every 401 needs
choices.why: Right. RFC 9110 requires one on every 401, and the orders send theirs.

choices.text: Its body tells a stranger the name of the header to send
choices.why: Naming the header is fine; the key itself is the secret, not where it goes.

prompt: Why should an API refuse its key in the query string, even when the key is correct?
hint: Look at what boxoffice's own log printed.

choices.text: Headers travel encrypted and addresses do not
choices.why: Over HTTPS both are encrypted on the wire; the leak happens after arrival.

choices.text: Addresses get logged by default; headers do not
choices.why: Right. boxoffice's log printed the key in plain text.

choices.text: A URL cannot carry the characters a key is made of
choices.why: Any key can be written in a URL; possibility is not the issue.

choices.text: A query string is read only by the browser, never by the server
choices.why: The server reads it; boxoffice's filter by date is a query parameter.

prompt: Match each field of the token response to what it says.
hint: The table in section 03.
right_distractors: the client secret, for the next request

prompt: Why must a token response carry `cache-control: no-store`?
hint: Who else sits between the program and the server?

choices.text: So that the token expires sooner
choices.why: Expiry is set by exp inside the token; caching does not change it.

choices.text: So that the client forgets the token after one request
choices.why: The header speaks to caches; the client keeps and reuses its token on purpose.

choices.text: So that every request fetches a new token
choices.why: A client fetches a token when the old one nears expiry, not on every request.

choices.text: So no cache keeps a live token and serves it to somebody else
choices.why: Right. OAuth requires it on the token endpoint, RFC 6749 §5.1.

prompt: The token response said "expires_in":900. How many minutes does a boxoffice token live?
hint: The field is in seconds.

prompt: Which statement about a JWT like boxoffice's is true?
hint: One line of Node decoded it.

choices.text: Its payload is encrypted with the server's secret
choices.why: It is signed, not encrypted; the secret only makes the signature.

choices.text: Anyone holding it can read its claims
choices.why: Right. The header and payload are base64url, readable by anybody.

choices.text: Only the token endpoint can decode its header
choices.why: The header decoded on your own machine with no secret at all.

choices.text: Its signature keeps the scope hidden from the client
choices.why: The scope is in the payload in plain sight; the signature protects it from change, not from reading.

prompt: The auditor's token, with its scope rewritten to include orders:write and its signature left alone, is sent as an order. What comes back, and why?
hint: Which does boxoffice check first, the signature or the claims?

choices.text: 403, because the auditor client is not allowed to write
choices.why: That would need the claims to be trusted first; the signature check comes before.

choices.text: 201, because the scope now says it may write
choices.why: That is the failure the test exists to catch, and boxoffice does not have it.

choices.text: 401 bad signature: it no longer matches
choices.why: Right. The edited token is refused before its claims are read.

choices.text: 401 token expired, because editing a token resets its exp
choices.why: exp was untouched; only scope changed.

prompt: A token fetched before boxoffice restarted still created an order afterwards. What does that tell you about withdrawing a token?
hint: How does boxoffice decide that a token is valid?

choices.text: It stays good until its exp, so tokens should be short-lived
choices.why: Right. Validity is recomputed from the secret and the clock; nothing lists tokens to remove.

choices.text: Restarting the server is the way to withdraw every token
choices.why: The capture showed the opposite: the old token worked after the restart.

choices.text: boxoffice saved its tokens to disk and reloaded them
choices.why: boxoffice keeps nothing on disk; orders vanished in the same restart.

choices.text: Tokens are checked against the token endpoint's list of issued tokens
choices.why: There is no list; the signature is recomputed with the secret.

prompt: Put the steps of the expiry test in order.
hint: The lifetime is shortened before the token exists.
items: use it at once and expect 201
use it again and expect 401 token expired

prompt: The auditor's valid token tries to create an order. What does boxoffice answer?
hint: The server knows who is asking.

choices.text: 401, because the auditor is not allowed to create
choices.why: 401 is for a caller the server does not know; this token is valid.

choices.text: 403 insufficient_scope
choices.why: Right. Known caller, act refused, and the header says which scope was missing.

choices.text: 404, because the auditor cannot see orders
choices.why: 404 came from reading another client's order, not from creating one.

choices.text: 422, because the body is not valid for an auditor
choices.why: The body is the same one ci-tests sent successfully; scope is checked before the body.

prompt: The auditor, with scope orders:read, gets 404 for ord-1001, which ci-tests created. What should the report say?
hint: Is the code wrong, or is the requirement unclear?

choices.text: That it is a defect, because the answer must be 403
choices.why: 403 would confirm the order exists; 404 is a deliberate way of giving nothing away.

choices.text: Nothing, because ord-1001 had already been cancelled
choices.why: It was cancelled only at the end of the section, after these requests.

choices.text: Ask whether that is what was intended
choices.why: Right. The code is consistent; whether it matches the intent is the owners' question.

choices.text: That the auditor's token had expired
choices.why: An expired token gets 401, not 404.

prompt: boxoffice answers `Authorization: bearer <a valid token>` with 401 no bearer token. What is your verdict?

choices.text: Correct: header values are case-sensitive
choices.why: The token is; the scheme name before it is not.

choices.text: Correct: the client should have spelt the token in capitals
choices.why: The token was exactly the one that worked; only the scheme word changed.

choices.text: A defect: the scheme name is case-insensitive
choices.why: Right. bearer and Bearer are the same scheme, and the fix is one toLowerCase().

choices.text: A defect: a malformed header should be answered with 400
choices.why: The header is well formed; the server simply misread it.

prompt: Which of these requests did boxoffice answer with 401?
hint: 401 means the credential was missing or not the kind this door takes.

choices.text: the staff key on an order
choices.why: Right. The orders want a bearer token, so the key counts as nothing.

choices.text: the ci-tests token on the sales report
choices.why: Right. The report wants its key, and a token is not one.

choices.text: the auditor creating an order
choices.why: That was 403: the caller is known and the act refused.

choices.text: the auditor reading ord-1001
choices.why: That was 404: the order is not the auditor's.

choices.text: a request with no token reading an order
choices.why: Right. No credential at all is the plainest 401.

prompt: Why does an app on a phone sign people in without a client secret?
hint: What is an Android package?

choices.text: OAuth forbids client secrets in every kind of client
choices.why: Servers keep secrets legitimately, as ci-tests does; only public clients go without.

choices.text: Every user holds a copy of the app's contents
choices.why: Right. A secret every user has a copy of is not a secret.

choices.text: The secret would expire whenever the app is updated
choices.why: Secrets do not expire with app versions; extraction is the problem.

choices.text: Phones cannot send a secret over HTTPS
choices.why: They can; the trouble is keeping it, not sending it.

prompt: Another app on the phone intercepts the authorization code in step 4. Why can it not get a token with it?
hint: What does step 5 send that never passed through the browser?

choices.text: The code is encrypted so that only the right app can read it
choices.why: The code is not encrypted for anyone; what protects it is a second value.

choices.text: The code works only from the phone's own network address
choices.why: Nothing in the flow ties a code to an address; the verifier ties it to the app.

choices.text: It lacks the verifier whose SHA-256 is the challenge
choices.why: Right. The challenge travelled through the browser; the verifier never left the app.

choices.text: Codes expire before another app has time to use them
choices.why: Codes are short-lived, but minutes are plenty for another app; PKCE is what stops it.

prompt: Match each check of an authorization server to the answer it expects.
hint: The table at the end of section 06.

pairs.left: a code exchanged with another verifier

pairs.right: refused, and no redirect to it

pairs.left: a state the app never sent

right_distractors: a token, with a warning in the log

prompt: After boxoffice was started with --env-file=.env, the TOKEN fetched earlier got 401 bad signature. Why?
hint: Section 04 showed that a restart alone did not do this.

choices.text: Every restart invalidates the tokens issued before it
choices.why: Section 04's token worked after a plain restart; the secret is what changed here.

choices.text: The token had expired while .env was being written
choices.why: Expiry gives token expired, and this said bad signature.

choices.text: The server now checks signatures with another secret
choices.why: Right. The recomputed signature differs, so the token is refused.

choices.text: Node could not read .env, so it refuses every token
choices.why: A fresh token from the same server would be accepted; only the old one fails.

prompt: A colleague committed .env with the signing secret, noticed an hour later and removed the commit. What else has to happen?
hint: Who might have copied the repository in that hour?

choices.text: Nothing; once the commit is gone the secret is safe again
choices.why: Every clone made in that hour still holds it.

choices.text: Add .env to .gitignore, which removes it from the history
choices.why: .gitignore stops a file being added; it does nothing to what was already committed.

choices.text: Change the secret, everywhere it is used
choices.why: Right. Treat it as leaked; a new secret makes every copy of the old one useless.

choices.text: Make the repository private for a week
choices.why: Copies made while it was readable are not affected by its visibility now.

prompt: A pipeline fetches a token with curl and runs its steps under `bash -x`. The client secret is registered with the CI system as a secret. What will the log show?
hint: Which value was registered, and which was produced during the run?

choices.text: Nothing sensitive, because the CI hides every Authorization header
choices.why: It hides registered values, wherever they appear; it does not parse headers.

choices.text: The token readable, and the other value starred out
choices.why: Right. The token was fetched during the run, so nothing hides it unless the step masks it.

choices.text: Both in the clear, since bash -x bypasses all masking
choices.why: Masking is applied to the log output, including what bash -x prints.

choices.text: The token, but it is harmless once the run finishes
choices.why: It stays valid until exp, fifteen minutes for boxoffice, and the log is kept far longer.

prompt: The theatre adds GET /v1/reports/daily, protected by the same X-Api-Key. Which set of tests follows from this lesson?
hint: Section 02 had three requests and two more checks.

choices.text: The right key returns 200 and a report
choices.why: One test of the happy path tells you nothing about who else gets in.

choices.text: A wrong key expecting 403, and the right key expecting 200
choices.why: A wrong key leaves the caller unknown, which is 401; and the missing-key case is absent.

choices.text: None, wrong and right key; the key in the query refused; www-authenticate on the 401
choices.why: Right. The three requests, the leak check and the header the report endpoint forgot.

choices.text: A ci-tests token and an auditor token, each expecting 200
choices.why: Tokens are not the key; both should get 401 on a key-protected address.

prompt: A client library fetches a fresh token and retries whenever it gets a 403. What is wrong with that?
hint: What would the fresh token's scope be?

choices.text: A 403 refuses the client, and a fresh token with the same scope is refused again
choices.why: Right. Refetching suits a 401; a 403 needs more scope or a different client.

choices.text: Nothing, since a 403 means the token has expired
choices.why: Expiry is a 401 with token expired; a 403 comes with a valid token.

choices.text: It should retry on 404 instead, which is what scope errors return
choices.why: boxoffice's scope error is 403 insufficient_scope; its 404 hides other clients' orders.

choices.text: Only the timing: it should wait a few seconds first
choices.why: Waiting does not change the token's scope; the retry fails however long it waits.

prompt: Because boxoffice cannot withdraw a JWT before its exp, the safe choice is to give tokens a ___ lifetime.
hint: Fifteen minutes rather than a month.
